To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
routine DFE in asymptomatic patients does not detect serious ocular events.
routine dilated funduscopic examinations are not indicated at 10-year or even 5-year intervals in asymptotic individuals.
routine dilated funduscopic examinations in older, asymptomatic individuals have a very low likelihood of detecting vision-threatening conditions.

routine dilated fundoscopic exams should not be performed on asymptomatic patients.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
routine DFE in asymptomatic patients does not appear to be cost effective and should probably be abandoned.
asymptomatic older patients should be dilated at the time of initial evaluation, and that routine DFE thereafter is not indicated.

The main takeaway from our work is that
routine DFE is not needed in asymptomatic patients, even at 10-year interval.
routine DFE for asymptomatic patients is ineffective in altering the clinical course of peripheral retinal ﬂecks, retinal holes or tears, retinal detachments or intraocular tumors.
routine DFE is not effective in altering the course or outcome of incidental ﬁnds in older patients.
